title: ICache eviction experiments for long-context workloads (Mistral / Qwen / Llama)
content:
Purpose:
Run targeted experiments to understand how instruction/kv cache eviction policies (LRU variants, segmented policies) interact with model architecture (Llama / Mistral / Qwen) and MoE routing under long-context workloads. We want actionable mitigations for p95/p99 latency spikes and better steady-state throughput for sequences >= 16k tokens.

Background / motivation:
- Our continuous-batching runtime relies on sharded in-memory icache (per-shard KV cache keyed by (request_id, seq_pos) with token->kv slices). Eviction occurs when memory thresholds reached. Historically we used a global LRU across all shards.
- Long contexts + MoE routing introduce two pain points: (1) uneven per-expert locality (some experts see heavy reuse, others sparse), (2) attention memory footprint grows quadratically with sequence length for some internal buffers and linearly for KV cache but with high per-token size at 65k contexts.
- Model differences: Qwen (multi-query attention-like) shows lower per-step KV pressure but higher transient working set in attention matmuls; Mistral tends to have wider feedforward which increases activation staging; Llama (our 7B/13B variants) shows strong temporal locality for prefix prompts but is sensitive to cross-batch eviction due to cache reuse patterns.

Experiment summary (short):
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB for throughput tests, 1x H100-80GB for microbenchmarks.
- Runtime: serving-runtime v0.28.3 (icache-refactor branch), CUDA 12.2, cuBLAS/cuDNN as of 2024-10.
- Models tested: llama-13b (fp16), mistral-7b-instruct (fp16), qwen-14b (int8/quantized variant)
- Workloads: synthetic prefix reuse (repeating 1k-token instruction + varying 16k/32k/65k suffix), and multi-turn chat traces from production with occasional long-context jumps.

Key measurements collected:
- KV cache hit-rate (per-shard, per-expert for MoE)
- Eviction rate (entries/sec), object size distributions
- Throughput (tokens/sec) under steady-state and during bursty arrivals
- Latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) for decode steps after cache pressure events
- GPU memory usage and host staging (if fallback-to-host occurred)

Representative results (high level):
- Baseline (global LRU): under 16k sequences, all models stable and hit-rate > 95%; throughput ~ 2200 tok/s for llama-13b on A100.
- At 32k sequences: Qwen shows a ~12% throughput drop; Mistral ~18%; Llama ~8%. p99 latency spikes observed most frequently for Mistral.
- At 65k sequences: eviction churn skyrockets for global LRU; hit-rate drops to 68% (Mistral), 75% (Qwen), 82% (Llama). p99 increases 2.6x for Mistral and 1.9x for Qwen.
- MoE routing interactions: when using an MoE-style layer (simulated by routing tokens to 32 experts), certain experts become hot and their per-expert kv shards saturate memory and force eviction of older but still-needed prefixes. This caused repeated recompute of KV slices and 20-30% stall in throughput during bursts.

Detailed observations:
1) Access locality differs by model and workload:
   - Llama: prefix reuse is common; many requests reuse the same system prompt. Global LRU ends up evicting less-used cross-request KV entries, good for this pattern.
   - Qwen: decode inner loops tend to re-access a narrow window of recent tokens but have larger transient matmul working sets; eviction of KV entries is less harmful than eviction of transient activation buffers.
   - Mistral: poor prefix reuse in our traces + larger FFN activation staging means evictions are more costly (recomputation of FFN activations and reuploading).

2) Per-expert sharding helps but naive sharding -> per-expert LRU causes fragmentation:
   - Implementing per-expert LRU reduced cross-expert eviction (hot experts keep their hot entries) and improved hit-rate for hot experts from 40% -> 82% in the hottest 3 experts.
   - However, cold experts' shards can be underutilized and cause overall memory imbalance; global thresholds still triggered evictions on hot shards.

3) Segmented-LRU (time-decay segments) showed promise:
   - We bucketed cached entries into hot / warm / cold segments using recency and access frequency heuristics. Entries promoted to 'hot' were protected until hot occupancy threshold reached.
   - For long-context Mistral runs this reduced p99 by ~18% compared to baseline and increased global hit-rate by ~9%.

4) Pinning recent prefixes + small pinned buffer:
   - Allowing user-specified pinned prefixes (e.g., system prompt) with memory reservation gave consistent gains for Llama workloads (p95 down by ~10%). But pinned memory leaks if not managed with lifecycle APIs.

5) Proactive prefetching on routing decisions:
   - When MoE routing is deterministic per token prefix, prefetching the likely expert-kv shards for the next N tokens reduced stalls on hot experts by ~25% during bursts. Trade-off: prefetch increases transient memory use.

Experiment notes (commands & setup):
- Sample runner invocation (local microbench):
  ./run_benchmark --model llama-13b --ctx 32768 --batch 4 --seq-profile --report=/tmp/llama-icache-32k.json

- Profiling hooks used: icache.hits(), eviction_trace.log, nvprof/cupti samples for kernel time slices.

Actionable recommendations (short-term / medium-term):
- Short-term (next 2 sprints):
  1) Implement segmented-LRU with simple hot/warm/cold buckets (configurable thresholds).
  2) Add API for application-level pinning of prompt prefixes and automatic TTL eviction.
  3) Add per-expert memory accounting for MoE layers and trigger early backpressure to avoid global eviction cascades.

- Medium-term (quarter):
  1) Work on adaptive prefetching tied to routing prediction confidence (only prefetch when model/dev confidence > threshold).
  2) Explore hybrid eviction policies that combine frequency (LFU) for per-expert shards with recency for global pool.
  3) Investigate selective checkpointing of FFN activations for Mistral flows to reduce recompute cost when evicted.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How does H100 memory model (cuda caching allocator behavior) impact our eviction thresholds compared to A100? Need cross-device repeat runs.
- For Qwen quantized variants, does smaller per-token KV payload shift the break-even point for prefetching vs eviction?
- Can we expose a per-route memory hint (ideal reserved bytes) through the API so high-reuse routes can reserve small pinned caches?
- Add unit tests for per-expert accounting and simulation harness for worst-case routing distributions.

Appendix: quick numeric snapshot (example run, A100)
- Workload: synthetic repeat prompt + 32k suffix, batch=4 decode
- Llama-13b: tokens/sec=2174, hit-rate=82.1%, p95=245ms, p99=412ms, evictions/sec=18
- Qwen-14b (quant): tokens/sec=1930, hit-rate=75.2%, p95=282ms, p99=510ms, evictions/sec=24
- Mistral-7b: tokens/sec=1790, hit-rate=68.4%, p95=330ms, p99=680ms, evictions/sec=37

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an experimental log; numbers will vary by model flavor and infra. Focus review on the suggested eviction policy changes and per-expert accounting design.
- If we prioritize pinned-prefix API, product/console will need UX for TTL and visibility (how much memory pinned).

References and related tickets:
- See linked PR/issue above for the icache-refactor branch.
- Related: JIRA-RT-1178 (MoE latency regression), JIRA-RT-1153 (cache TTL feature request).

End of note.
